steps.action:
The first storm of autumn arrived without warning.

Just after dusk, as the last gray light seeped away from the sea, the sky split itself into rough, jagged seams of lightning. Rain came down in sudden sheets, the kind that made the ocean look as if it were boiling up from within. The waves began to rise and fold over themselves, pushing their white shoulders against the rocks.

In the glass room of the lighthouse, Elias turned the key in the control box and watched the great lamp ignite—once, twice, and then fully—its beam slicing a clean arc through the rain.

He did this every night, but never exactly the same way. The routine had its rituals, its small variations. He always muttered a greeting to the light, as if it were a temperamental animal. He always checked the panes for new hairline cracks. He always timed the rotation by his own count, trusting his inner metronome more than the aging gears.

The Beacon of Holt Head had been his responsibility for twenty-seven years. In that time, the town on the mainland had grown from a cluster of salt-box houses into something like a small, busy jaw of lights. The fishing fleet had become a marina and yacht club. The old gas station had become a low, glass-fronted café that boasted “harbor views” and “artisanal espresso.”

But out here, on the narrow knuckle of rock that knifed into the Atlantic, the lighthouse stayed mostly the same—taller than it needed to be, older than it had any right to be, and stubborn in both respects.

The light turned, measured and unhurried. Seventeen seconds between flashes. Elias had it memorized, not just as a number, but as a feeling. Long enough to take three slow breaths. Long enough to hear one wave strike, hiss, and recede.

He moved around the lantern room, checking the seals, touching the metal. The windows were old thick glass, rippled in places, so that the storm outside looked slightly distorted, as if he watched it through memory’s own uneven lens.

The radio on the shelf below the window crackled with a distant voice.

“…coast guard station…visibility low…repeat, visibility low…”

Elias turned the knob with two fingers until the sound clarified.

“…storm front moving faster than forecast…all small craft advised to return to harbor. This is Coast Guard Station Harrow. Over.”

Elias lifted the radio, pressed the transmit button, and spoke with the slow care of someone who often spent days without needing to talk at all.

“Holt Head Light, Keeper Elias Rowan. Light operational. Visibility reduced, but beam clear. No vessels in visual range. Over.”

“Copy that, Holt Head. Keep an eye out. They lost a pleasure craft from Harrow Marina an hour back. Some idiot thought he could outrun the weather. Report any contacts. Over.”

Elias frowned at the rain-choked horizon. No lights. No shadows against the pale, restless underbelly of the clouds.

“Understood. Keeping watch. Over and out.”

He returned the radio to its shelf and stood still for a moment, letting the storm’s sounds press in through the glass: the rumble of thunder too low to be heard as anything but vibration, the slap of rain, the steady mechanical turning of the lens assembly behind him.

He liked storms, in a way. They gave shape to his solitude. On calm, clear nights, the sea looked like absence. On nights like this, it was present, angry, alive.

He took the iron stair down one level to the watch room. The walls here were thick stone painted the color of old bones. A desk, a chair, a narrow cot for brief naps that were never quite restful. A weather chart pinned to a cork board. A photograph of a woman in black-and-white, her hair pinned back, eyes candid and almost amused, looking at something beyond the camera.

Lena. Twenty-seven years ago, she had taken the photograph of him that sat on her dressing table in the house in town. Twenty-seven years ago, she had promised she’d learn to like the sea if he learned to like the idea of “days off.” Twenty-six years ago, her car had not made it through the first patch of black ice of winter.

The storm outside intensified, as if summoned by the direction of his thoughts. The glass in the watch room window rattled. Thunder rolled over the roof like a slow, heavy object being dragged.

Elias sat at the desk and opened the logbook. The day’s entries were already there: sunrise time; noon weather; evening check of the lens, the backup generator, the fuel levels. He added a new line in his angular, patient handwriting.

“1923 hours – Storm front arrived from WNW faster than predicted. High wind. Visibility < 0.5 nm. Light operational, rotation normal. Harrow CG reports missing small craft.”

He paused, the pen hovering, then added: “Will maintain heightened watch.”

He capped the pen and listened to the almost theatrical rage of the wind.

Years ago, before automation, before satellite navigation, keepers would staff Holt Head in teams of three. There had been a supply boat twice a week, and a rotation on and off the rock so that no one spent too long staring at nothing but stone and water.

But time and funding and new technology had pared that down. There was still a supply boat, but now it came once a week. There were still maintenance crews from the Coast Guard, but now they came only when something broke badly enough that Elias could not cajole it back into service himself. And there was still a keeper.

Just one.

There were systems in place, of course. Backups for the backups. Automatic starters, fail-safes, satellite feeds. In theory, the lighthouse could almost run itself.

Elias had read that phrase once, in a report. “Run itself.” As if the sea would politely accept the notion.

He stood again, the old ache rising in his knees, and climbed back up to the lantern room. The climb was second nature. He did it in the dark often, when power cut out and he had to get the backup running by flashlight. He had the steps counted, the height known in his bones.

At the top, he walked the narrow ring around the lamp, eyes searching for anything—anything—that did not belong in the layered darkness of waves and rain and sky.

On his second circuit, he saw it: a brief, odd glow far out to the southeast. Not lightning. Too steady, too small. A light that appeared and disappeared between the swells.

He waited, breath held, as the great lamp completed another slow revolution, its beam cutting over that patch of water like the sweep of an enormous white sword.

There. Again. Flickering, bobbing. Then gone behind a fold of sea.

He reached for the binoculars hanging from a hook. The lenses fogged briefly as he lifted them to his eyes; he wiped them with his sleeve, hands surprisingly steady, and leaned his forehead against the glass.

At first, there was nothing but a curtain of rain. A flash of lightning turned it briefly to silver threads. Then the beam passed over the spot again, and this time he caught it: the upturned belly of a small motorboat, the white hull smudged with something dark—seaweed, oil, he could not tell. The light he had seen came from somewhere just beyond, low and intermittent: a handheld flare or a flashlight.

“Damn,” he whispered, not as an oath but as a statement of recognition. The missing pleasure craft. People in the water.

He lowered the binoculars and grabbed the radio.

“Holt Head to Harrow CG, over.”

Static for a moment, then: “Harrow CG. Go ahead, Holt Head.”

“Visual on what appears to be overturned small craft approximately…” He measured the angle out of instinct, eyes flicking from the lamp to the lined chart in his mind. “Approximately one point three nautical miles southeast of Holt Head, bearing one-four-two. Intermittent light source, likely flare or torch. Weather reducing visibility and complicating estimate, but there are survivors in the water. Over.”

The pause was longer this time. He pictured faces he did not know bending over maps, fingers tracing distances, minds calculating risk.

“Copy, Holt Head. One point three nautical mi SE, bearing one-four-two. We’ve got a cutter already heading your way. Sea state’s getting ugly. We’ll vector them to your coordinates. Can you maintain visual?”

Elias looked at the storm, which had no intention of lessening its venting.

“I’ll do my best. Light beam can help them orient. I’ll also deploy auxiliary flare if necessary. Over.”

“Appreciate it, Elias. Stay safe up there. Harrow out.”

Stay safe. The phrase always struck him as faintly ridiculous, like telling a man standing in the path of a glacier not to catch a cold.

He set the radio down and walked a full, tight circle of the lantern room, eyes locked southeast. Every time the light swung that way, he lifted the binoculars and scanned.

The sea had become a confusion of black humps and white scars. Rain hammered the glass so hard it was a near-constant roar. Sometimes he caught a fleeting mark—the curve of the overturned hull, the flash of the weaker light. Once, he thought he saw an arm, a hand rising from the water, but it vanished before he could be sure.

He could not go out there himself. Regulations were clear: the keeper did not leave the station in conditions like this, not in the small utility skiff moored on the leeward side of the rock. He was not a rescue swimmer, not a hero. He was a point of reference. A guardian of information, not of flesh.

But there are regulations, and then there are the questions you have to ask yourself later in the quiet hours you used to share with someone else.

He lifted the radio again. “Holt Head to Harrow CG, over.”

“Harrow here, go ahead.”

“Estimate on cutter ETA to my position? Over.”

“Cutter Severn is ten minutes out from Holt Head in this weather. They’ll need another six or seven to make that bearing.”

Seventeen minutes. In this water. He pictured the night Lena had taken that last drive, thinking the roads were just wet. How many minutes had made the difference between “she might make it” and “there’s nothing we can do”?

He knew the water here intimately. He knew where the currents pinwheeled, where submerged shelves of stone lay in ambush. He also knew the short, narrow path from the lighthouse door down the slick cut stairs to the boathouse, and how many times he had walked it sure-footed in better weather.

The beam turned, slicing through rain and spray. For a brief second it illuminated the overturned boat and the weak, wildly swinging point of light near it. Closer than before. Whether that meant the survivors were drifting toward the rock or he was noticing more details in the storm’s underpainting, he could not be sure.

The question was not whether he could go. He could. The question was whether he would live with himself if he did not.

He set the radio down deliberately, picked up a small waterproof flashlight and his heavy oilskin coat from the hook by the stairs, and began to descend.

The wind pressed against the tower as if it wanted to push it sideways into the sea. The stone steps shuddered faintly. Down through the watch room, where the photograph on the wall trembled in its frame, blurring her smile. Down past the equipment room, where the backup generator hummed in steady ignorance of the tempest above.

At the ground level, the heavy wooden door fought him. He leaned his weight into it, shoulder protesting, until it cracked open and a slab of wet air punched its way in. Rain hit his face like thrown gravel.

He stepped out.

The path from the lighthouse to the boathouse was carved directly into the rock, protected on one side by a chest-high stone wall slick with moss and lichen. Water pooled and ran in miniature streams across the uneven surface. The sky had gone from mere darkness to something closer to a moving ceiling of slate.

He moved slowly, one hand on the wall, the other gripping the flashlight. Lightning lit the world in freeze-frames: the jagged foam as waves crashed against the far side of the rock, the shadowed line of the mainland a smudge on the horizon, the solitary, upright shape of the lighthouse he had just left, its windows bright, its lamp turning tirelessly.

The boathouse door was a sheet of corrugated metal rigged with a heavy latch. He wrestled it open and ducked inside. The roar outside became a muffled, angry echo.

The small utility skiff lay in its cradle, bobbing fractionally as the water in the sheltered inlet rose and fell. A modest outboard engine hung off its stern. It was a workboat, plain and practical, with just enough freeboard to make a round trip to the mainland in fair weather without exciting too much comment.

He had always told the maintenance crew that the skiff was there solely for supply runs, emergency trips to town for parts, or evacuations if the light failed catastrophically. They had nodded. No one had written down the word “only” on any form.

His fingers found the life vest by habit. He slipped it on, tightened the straps until the fabric dug into his ribs. The ritual of it steadied him.

Outside, thunder boomed, and the boathouse shivered.

He lowered the skiff with the electric winch, watching the short line of rope play out. The boat touched the water, rocked, settled. He climbed down the ladder, boots finding rungs slick with algae, and dropped into the boat, bending his knees to absorb the landing.

For a moment, the bobbing, the smell of wet fuel and salt, the taste of iron in his mouth all collided with memory. Another boat, another storm, decades earlier. A younger Elias, hands shaking as he tried to fix a jammed fuel line while his father cursed the sky for closing in too early.

“You always think you have more time than you do,” his father had said that night, voice half swallowed by the wind. “The sea has its own clock.”

He shook the memory away, turned the key, and felt relief when the engine sputtered, coughed, and caught, settling into a rough but workable vibration.

He cast off, pushing away from the boathouse wall with the heel of his hand, and guided the skiff around to the seaward side of the rock, where the swell was already higher.

Out there, beyond the immediate shelter of Holt Head, the enormity of the storm asserted itself. The skiff rose and fell like a toy on an old giant’s chest. Wind-driven spray needled his cheeks; rain turned everything beyond a dozen meters into a shifting, noisy blur.

Above, the lighthouse’s beam swept in its steady arc. Every seventeen seconds, it reappeared, washing over the sea with its cold, decisive light.

He aimed for the bearing he had called in: one-four-two. Without instruments worth trusting in this weather, he relied on the light and his own sense of angle. He was a lighthouse keeper, after all. His body was trained to know where the beam would be before it arrived.

When it passed ahead of him, he adjusted a degree or two, coaxing the skiff along the edge of its path, as if following the faint trace of a line drawn on the water.

Waves slapped the hull, sometimes with enough force to stagger him. He kept one hand on the tiller, the other braced on the side. The bow cut through some waves, climbed others reluctantly. Once, a crest broke over the bow and poured cold water into the boat up to his shins. He swore, but the engine held.

“Just a little further,” he murmured aloud, though there was no one to hear above the storm. “You stay with me, old girl. Just a little further.”

Another sweep of the lighthouse beam caught an upraised shape ahead—a piece of wood? No. The overturned boat, larger now, close enough that he could see the letters on its side in brief, harsh illumination. LILLY JANE. The painted curve of the name vanishing as the hull rolled.

To port, lower, was the faltering light of a flare burning stubbornly reddish through the rain. It jerked and dipped, sometimes vanishing entirely behind a wave.

He altered course that way, teeth clenched, and yelled out, “Holt Head keeper! Call out if you hear me!”

For a moment, there was only the storm’s reply. Then, faint and ragged and almost torn apart by the wind, came a shout.

“Here! Over—here!”

His heart did something complicated and painful in his chest. It had been years since he had heard a human voice this close that did not come from a radio or a maintenance crew.

The beam passed over them again. In the light he saw two figures clinging to a partially deflated life raft, their faces pale oval blurs. One of them waved the dying flare. The other seemed barely conscious, head lolling, legs trailing in the water.

“I see you!” Elias roared, though they could not possibly hear the words more than as another noise among many. He throttled back as he approached, wanting to avoid crushing them in the surge.

The skiff heaved. A wave hit the stern and spun it half around. He fought the tiller, muscles burning, until the bow was facing them again. The engine coughed but did not quit.

“Grab the gunwale when I come alongside!” he shouted, gesturing, hoping the universal language of desperation and help would translate.

On the next lift of the waves, the skiff slid closer to them, the raft bumping against the hull with a hollow thud. The man with the flare dropped it to grab for the boat. The flare hit the water and died like a wounded animal, hissing out in a puff of steam.

Up close, Elias could see them better: the man in his thirties, maybe, hair plastered to his head, eyes wide and bloodshot; the woman, younger, limp in her life jacket, lips an alarming shade close to blue.

“Get her in first!” Elias yelled, already reaching down.

Together they found the right rhythm with the waves: when the skiff rose and the raft dipped, he hooked his arms under the woman’s and hauled, the man lifting from below. Her weight was awkward, her limbs stiff. For a second, he thought he would lose his footing, but a contrary lurch of the boat slammed him against the gunwale, anchoring him with pain instead of balance.

She came over the side in a tumble of wet fabric and cold flesh, landing half on his boots. He fell backward, grunting, the wind knocked from him. She lay there, eyes half open, unfocused.

“Anna! Anna, breathe for God’s sake—” the man shouted, half inside the boat now, fingers still clamped on the raft with one hand as if afraid to let go of both worlds at once.

“Get in!” Elias barked, scrabbling to his knees. “We have to move!”
